Sequential Decisions: The Stagecoach Problem

Four Legs from A to J

  • A traveler crosses from town A to town J in four legs by stagecoach
  • Each leg needs a life insurance policy; the number on an arc is its cost
  • Which route costs the least in total?
  • Revisiting the shortest path problem

Hillier and Lieberman’s prototype (Sec. 11.1): a gold-rush traveler in the 1800s, insured leg by leg, with the premium set by how dangerous the road is. The stages are the legs; each choice of town decides which towns are reachable next. That coupling is the whole topic.

The Cheapest Next (Greedy heuristic) Leg Misses the Optimum

Cheapest next leg: A–B–F–I–J, \({2 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 13}\)

Better: A–D–F–I–J, \({3 + 1 + 3 + 4 = 11}\)

Paying 1 more on leg 1 saves 3 on leg 2.

The greedy rule looks one leg ahead. The cheap first leg to B leads to expensive second legs (4, 6, 7). Ask the class for a better route before the second click.

Enumerate, or Use the Stages

  • All routes: \({3 \times 3 \times 2 = 18}\). Three cost 11; the next best cost 13
  • With 10 stages of 10 towns each: \({10^9}\) routes to add up

The idea of dynamic programming

  • Solve the problem from the last stage: one leg from J.
  • Then enlarge it one stage at a time, reusing the answer for the stages already solved.
  • Each arc is used in one addition: 20 here, about 1,000 for 10 stages of 10 towns.

Count for the large case: 9 stage transitions of 10 x 10 arcs plus the first and last stages, about 900 to 1,000 additions, against a billion routes. The answer from J backward is also an answer for every town, so a traveler thrown off course still knows what to do.

Stages, States and the Bellman Recursion

Stages, States and Controls

Term Symbol Stagecoach
Stage \({k = 0, \dots, N - 1}\) Leg \({k + 1}\); \({N = 4}\)
State \({x_k}\) Town at the start of the leg
Control \({u_k \in U_k(x_k)}\) Next town
System \({x_{k+1} = f_k(x_k, u_k)}\) \({x_{k+1} = u_k}\)

The state summarizes the past information relevant for the future. The system \({f_k}\) is the state transition function.

At stage 1 in state C: \({U_1(\text{C}) = \{\text{E}, \text{F}, \text{G}\}}\).

Bertsekas’s notation (Dynamic Programming and Optimal Control, Vol. I, ch. 1): stages count from k = 0, so x_0 is the start and x_N the end. Control is his word for the decision. The state is defined by what the rest of the problem needs: here only the current town matters, not the route that reached it.

Costs, Cost-to-Go and Policies

Term Symbol Stagecoach
Stage cost \({g_k(x_k, u_k)}\) Premium of the leg
Terminal cost \({g_N(x_N)}\) \({g_4(\text{J}) = 0}\)
Total cost, additive in the basic problem \({g_N(x_N) + \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} g_k(x_k, u_k)}\) Sum of the four premiums
Optimal cost-to-go \({J^*_k(x_k)}\) Least cost from \({x_k}\) to J
Policy \({\pi = \{\mu_0, \dots, \mu_{N-1}\}}\), \({u_k = \mu_k(x_k)}\) Next town from every town

Cost-to-go

\({J^*_k(x_k)}\): the least cost of the stages left, from \({x_k}\); the value function of the tail

A policy is a rule, one function mu_k per stage, that names a control for every state. Bertsekas minimizes cost; a problem that maximizes profit, person-years or a probability uses max in the same algorithm.

The DP Algorithm

Start at the end, then go backward one stage at a time:

\[ \begin{alignat*}{2} J^*_N(x_N) & {}= g_N(x_N) \\[4pt] J^*_k(x_k) & {}= \min_{u_k \in U_k(x_k)} \Big[\, g_k(x_k, u_k) + J^*_{k+1}\big(f_k(x_k, u_k)\big) \Big] && \qquad k = N - 1, \dots, 0 \end{alignat*} \]

  • The bracket is the Q-factor \({Q^*_k(x_k, u_k)}\): control \({u_k}\) now, then the best from the state it leads to. The next section computes it for every \({x_k}\) and \({u_k}\), one table per stage
  • Stagecoach: \({J^*_k(x_k) = \min_{u_k} \big[ c_{x_k u_k} + J^*_{k+1}(u_k) \big]}\), \({J^*_4(\text{J}) = 0}\)
  • \({J^*_0(\text{A})}\) is the least total cost; the minimizers \({\mu^*_k(x_k)}\) form an optimal policy

Bertsekas calls this the DP algorithm; it solves every tail subproblem, from every state, not only the one that starts at A. The star marks “optimal over the remaining stages”. The terminal condition J*_4(J) = 0: at J the trip is over.

The Principle of Optimality

Bellman (1957)

An optimal policy has the property that whatever the initial state and initial decision are, the remaining decisions must constitute an optimal policy with regard to the state resulting from the first decision.

  • The tail of an optimal policy is optimal for the tail subproblem that starts at \({x_k}\): the future ignores how the process got there

The quotation is Bellman’s statement of the principle (Dynamic Programming, 1957, ch. III). The bullet is Bertsekas’s form of it: the tail policy {mu*_k, …, mu*_N-1} is optimal for the tail subproblem. The diagram is the deterministic structure: the control moves the process to a state fully determined by x_k and u_k.

What Makes a Problem a Dynamic Program

  1. Stages \({k = 0, \dots, N - 1}\)
  2. A state \({x_k}\) that holds what the future needs to know of the past
  3. A control \({u_k \in U_k(x_k)}\): the action or decision at stage \({k}\)
  4. A system (or state transition function) \({x_{k+1} = f_k(x_k, u_k)}\)
  5. A cost that separates by stage: a sum, a product or a max; another function of the total goes in \({g_N}\), with the running total in the state
  6. The DP algorithm gives \({J^*_k}\) from \({J^*_{k+1}}\), last stage first

Deterministic dynamic programming

  • Part II adds a random disturbance \({w_k}\): \({x_{k+1} = f_k(x_k, u_k, w_k)}\)

Reading the Routes Forward

  • Stage 0: \({u^*_0}\) = C or D

Three optimal routes, cost 11

A–C–E–H–J

A–D–F–I–J

The tables are read forward: u*_0 from the stage 0 table, then the row of the town it leads to in the stage 1 table, and so on. B and G are off every optimal route, but their rows still say what to do if the traveler ends up there.

Dynamic Programming and the Shortest Path Algorithm

The stagecoach is a shortest path problem; lecture 06’s algorithm also finds 11.

Shortest path algorithm Dynamic programming
Order Nodes, nearest first Stages, last first
Work per step Scan the solved nodes’ neighbors One addition per arc
Networks Any, lengths \({\ge 0}\) Staged, lengths of any sign
Result Best paths from the origin A control \({\mu_k(x_k)}\) for every state

When the network comes in stages

Dynamic programming uses the stages: no search for the next nearest node, and the answer is a policy for every state.

Bertsekas (lecture 3 of his MIT 6.231 slides): a deterministic finite-state DP is a shortest path problem on its staged graph, and the DP algorithm is one way to solve it. Dijkstra needs nonnegative lengths; a staged network has no cycles, so dynamic programming handles negative premiums (rebates) as well. The policy view matters once chance enters in Part II: the next state is not known in advance, so a plan must say what to do in every state.

Distribution of Effort: Allocating Medical Teams

Five Medical Teams, Three Countries

Additional person-years of life, in thousands
Teams Country 1 Country 2 Country 3
0 0 0 0
1 45 20 50
2 70 45 70
3 90 75 80
4 105 110 100
5 120 150 130
  • A health council has five medical teams for three low-income countries
  • Teams stay intact: each country gets a whole number of them
  • Decide how many teams each country gets, to maximize the total person-years of life added

Hillier and Lieberman’s Example 2 (the World Health Council). The measure is increased life expectancy times population. Country 2’s column grows slowly and then fast: no simple ranking of countries works.

Countries as Stages, Teams Left as the State

  • Stage \({k}\): country \({k + 1}\); control \({u_k}\): its teams
  • State \({x_k}\): teams still free; \({x_0 = 5}\), \({x_{k+1} = x_k - u_k}\)
  • Stage reward \({g_k(u_k)}\): country \({k + 1}\)’s column

\[ \begin{alignat*}{2} J^*_k(x_k) & {}= \max_{u_k = 0, \dots, x_k} \big[\, g_k(u_k) + J^*_{k+1}(x_k - u_k) \big] \end{alignat*} \]

With \({J^*_3 = 0}\), country 3 takes every team left: \({J^*_2(x_2) = g_2(x_2)}\).

An arc from \({x_1}\) to \({x_2}\) earns \({g_1(x_1 - x_2)}\): the best path is the best allocation.

Distribution of Effort Problems

Distribution of effort

One resource shared among activities, each with its own return table \({g_k(u_k)}\).

  • The returns need only combine stage by stage: a sum here, a product in the research-teams example. Each \({g_k}\) can be any table: country 2’s rises slowly, then fast, so no ranking of the countries works
  • Whole teams cost nothing extra: the states and controls are the integers 0 to 5
  • Other examples: sales reps to regions, scientists to research teams, an ad budget to media

Hillier and Lieberman, Sec. 11.3. As an integer program the same problem needs a binary for each country and team count (18 of them), one choice per country and a limit of 5 teams; the table enters as objective coefficients. The DP needs 6 states per stage and no linear form at all.

Knapsacks: Dynamic Versus Integer Programming

Loading a Truck

Load A B C D
Pallets 2 3 4 5
Pays ($100s) 7 11 10 12
Per pallet 3.5 3.67 2.5 2.4
  • The truck holds 7 pallets; each load goes whole or not at all
  • Best pay per pallet first: B, then A: \({11 + 7 = 18}\), 2 pallets empty

As an integer program (IP), \({x_i = 1}\) if load \({i}\) goes:

\[ \begin{alignat*}{3} \max~ & \rlap{7x_A + 11x_B + 10x_C + 12x_D} \\[4pt] \text{s.t.}~ & 2x_A + 3x_B + 4x_C + 5x_D & \quad & {}\le 7 \\ & x_A, x_B, x_C, x_D & \quad & {}\in \{0, 1\} \end{alignat*} \]

A knapsack problem: one constraint, yes-or-no items. Capital budgeting with one budget is the same model.

A carrier is offered four loads for one trip. The LP relaxation gives 23 (A, B and half of C), an upper bound; the IP optimum is 21. The greedy answer 18 leaves 2 pallets of room unused.

The Knapsack as a Dynamic Program

  • Stage \({k}\): load A, B, C, D for \({k = 0, \dots, 3}\); control \({u_k \in \{0, 1\}}\)
  • State \({x_k}\): pallets still free; \({x_0 = 7}\), \({x_{k+1} = x_k - a_k u_k}\)
  • \({u_k = 1}\) only if \({a_k \le x_k}\)

\[ \begin{alignat*}{2} J^*_k(x_k) & {}= \max_{u_k} \big[\, v_k\, u_k + J^*_{k+1}(x_k - a_k\, u_k) \big] \\[4pt] J^*_4(x_4) & {}= 0 \end{alignat*} \]

  • \({a_k}\): pallets; \({v_k}\): pay. States run from 0 to 7 at every stage but the first

Loads B and C: $2,100

All 7 pallets used. gurobipy on the IP: 21, the same loads.

Three Budgets Make the State a Vector

Capital budgeting: choose among 5 projects, each spending money in each of three years, with three yearly budgets of 150, 110 and 60 ($1,000s).

  • The state is the money left in each year: \({(b_1, b_2, b_3)}\)
  • In $1,000 steps: \({151 \times 111 \times 61 = 1{,}022{,}421}\) states per stage, against 8 for the truck

State spaces grow exponentially

The number of states grows exponentially with the number of state variables, which Bellman called “the curse of dimensionality”. By hand, the state must take a handful of values; three budgets are a job for the IP solver.

Bellman’s phrase is in the preface of Dynamic Programming (1957). This is lecture 02’s bookstore; the IP solves it instantly ($330,000). Dynamic programming pays off when the state is small and the stage returns are nonlinear or tabulated, as in the medical teams problem.

Dynamic Programming or Integer Programming

Dynamic programming Integer programming
Answer A policy: \({u_k = \mu_k(x_k)}\) in every state One plan for the data given
Costs Any \({g_k}\): a table, nonlinear, nonconcave Linear, or linearized with binaries
Integers Free: states and controls are listed Branch and bound, with a gap
Uncertainty \({E_{w_k}}\) inside the algorithm (Part II) A scenario tree (lecture 05)
Structure A cost that separates by stage; a state that sums up the past Any linear constraints
Size States grow exponentially in the state variables Thousands of variables; time varies

Sources: Bertsekas, MIT 6.231 slides (2015), lecture 1: DP optimizes over policies, functions mu_k(x_k); “in deterministic problems open loop is as good as closed loop”; the value of information appears only with uncertainty. Lecture 8, practical difficulties of DP: the curse of dimensionality (exponential growth in the number of state and control variables) and the curse of modeling. Stochastic programming with recourse (lecture 05, Birge and Louveaux) handles uncertainty in an LP or IP through scenarios; a multistage tree grows exponentially with the stages. The two methods meet: Martin, Rardin and Campbell (1990) write a discrete DP as a path LP on its state graph, which tightens IP formulations. Knapsack: both give 21. Capital budgeting with three budgets: a job for the IP solver.

Plans and Policies: Open and Closed Loop

  • A plan fixes \({u_0, \dots, u_{N-1}}\) in advance (open loop). A policy picks \({u_k = \mu_k(x_k)}\) after it sees \({x_k}\) (closed loop)
  • Deterministic problem: every \({x_k}\) is known in advance, so the best plan costs the same as the best policy
  • Under uncertainty the policy costs less or the same: it uses what each stage reveals. Part II’s auction bids by the engines still needed

An integer program can act as a policy

Re-solve it at every stage with the new state (a rolling horizon), or write a scenario tree that branches on what can happen (lecture 05).

Bertsekas, MIT 6.231 slides (2015), lecture 1, “Significance of feedback”: in deterministic problems open loop is as good as closed loop; with uncertainty the difference is the value of information. In the stagecoach the policy still says what to do in a town off the optimal route. Powell (2019) calls re-solving a deterministic model at each step a lookahead policy.

Part II: Continuous States and Probabilistic Recursions

When the state is a number on a line, and when chance picks the next state

Discrete and Continuous States: The Endpoint Argument

Three New Products, One Plant

Product 1 2 3
Start-up cost \({c}\) 3 2 0
Marginal net revenue \({r}\) 2 3 1
Capacity per unit 20% 40% 20%
  • Starting a product costs \({c}\) once; each unit then adds \({r}\)
  • Product 1 sells at most 3 units; products 2 and 3 sell all they make
  • Decide how many units of each to make, to maximize net revenue minus start-up costs

(a) Integer units. (b) Divisible units. A past Exam 2 problem, 60 of 100 points.

Problem 2 of a past Exam 2; its solution file calls it Problem 11-2 and works it in Hillier and Lieberman’s notation. The capacity percentages are multiples of 20, which is what makes the integer state small: five blocks of 20%.

Integer Production: The State in 20% Blocks

  • Stage \({k}\): product \({k + 1}\); control \({u_k}\): units made
  • State \({x_k}\): 20% blocks of capacity left: \({x_0 = 5}\), \({x_1 = 5 - u_0}\), \({x_2 = x_1 - 2u_1}\)
  • Profit of \({u_k}\) units: \({g_k(u_k) = r\,u_k - c}\) if \({u_k > 0}\), and 0 if \({u_k = 0}\), with product \({k + 1}\)’s \({r}\) and \({c}\)

\[ \begin{alignat*}{2} J^*_k(x_k) & {}= \max_{u_k} \big[\, g_k(u_k) + J^*_{k+1}(x_k - a_k\, u_k) \big] \\[4pt] J^*_2(x_2) & {}= x_2 \end{alignat*} \]

  • \({a_k}\): blocks per unit, 1, 2, 1. Product 3 has no start-up cost, so it takes every block left

Stage 1, x_1 = 4: u_1 = 0 gives 0 + 4; u_1 = 1 gives (3 - 2) + J*_2(2) = 1 + 2 = 3; u_1 = 2 gives (6 - 2) + 0 = 4. Ties are kept. The start-up cost is why u_1 = 1 never wins: one unit of product 2 earns 3 - 2 = 1, the same as the two blocks it uses would earn as product 3.

Three Optimal Plans

Read every tie forward

A tie in \({u^*_k}\) branches the forward pass. The exam asks for all optimal plans.

Divisible Units: Only the Endpoints Matter

  • \({x_k}\): percent of capacity left; \({x_0 = 100}\)
  • Product 3: \({J^*_2(x_2) = x_2/20}\)
  • Product 2: \({3u_1 - 2 + (x_1 - 40u_1)/20}\), linear in \({u_1 > 0}\)
  • Compare the endpoints: \({u_1 = 0}\) gives \({x_1/20}\), and \({u_1 = x_1/40}\) gives \({3x_1/40 - 2}\)
  • Equal at \({x_1 = 80}\): product 2 only if \({x_1 \ge 80}\)

The exam solution’s argument: the profit is linear in u_k except for the start-up term, so the maximum over 0 <= u_1 <= x_1/40 is at an end of the interval. The red band is J*_1(x_1): x_1/20 up to 80 and 3 x_1/40 - 2 above.

Divisible Units: Stage 1 and the Plan

\(Q^*_0(100, u_0) = 2u_0 - 3 + J^*_1(100 - 20u_0)\) for \({0 < u_0 \le 3}\), and \({J^*_1(100)}\) for \({u_0 = 0}\).

  • \({u_0 = 0}\): \({J^*_1(100) = 3(100)/40 - 2 =}\) 5.5
  • \({u_0 = 3}\): \({6 - 3 + J^*_1(40) = 3 + 2 = 5}\)
  • \({Q^*_0}\) rises on \({0 < u_0 \le 3}\), so these two are the candidates

Divisible optimum: 5.5

\({u_0 = 0}\), so \({x_1 = 100 \ge 80}\) and \({u_1 = 100/40 = 2.5}\); then \({x_2 = 0}\), \({u_2 = 0}\). Make 2.5 units of product 2 only. Divisibility adds 0.5 to the integer optimum.

On 0 < u_0 <= 1, x_1 is in [80, 100) and Q*_0 = 2.5 + 0.5 u_0; on 1 <= u_0 <= 3, x_1 is in [40, 80] and Q*_0 = 2 + u_0. Both pieces rise, so u_0 = 3 is the best positive level and it loses to u_0 = 0. gurobipy, with a binary for each start-up: 5.5 at (0, 2.5, 0).

Continuous States by Calculus: Employment Levels

The Local Job Shop

  • Workers needed each season: the chart, from this spring to the next
  • No overtime and no inventory: custom orders
  • A worker above the requirement costs $2,000 a season
  • Changing the level costs $200 × (change)²
  • Part-time workers make fractional levels possible

Hillier and Lieberman’s Example 4. Hiring and training is costly, so management dislikes swings; idle workers are costly too. The question is how far to cut the workforce in the slack seasons.

Seasons as Stages, Last Season’s Level as the State

  • Stage \({k}\): season, \({k = 0}\) summer to \({k = 3}\) spring; control \({u_k}\): workers employed; \({u_k \ge r_k}\) and \({u_3 = 255}\)
  • State \({x_k = u_{k-1}}\), last season’s level; \({x_0 = 255}\)

\[ \begin{alignat*}{2} J^*_k(x_k) & {}= \min_{r_k \le u_k \le 255} \big[\, 200(u_k - x_k)^2 + 2000(u_k - r_k) + J^*_{k+1}(u_k) \big] \\[4pt] J^*_3(x_3) & {}= 200(255 - x_3)^2 \end{alignat*} \]

A continuous state

\({x_k}\) can be any number in an interval: no table can list it. Each \({J^*_k}\) is a formula in \({x_k}\), minimized by setting a derivative to 0.

Winter by Calculus

\(Q^*_2(x_2, u_2) = 200(u_2 - x_2)^2 + 2000(u_2 - 200) + 200(255 - u_2)^2\)

\[ \frac{\partial Q^*_2}{\partial u_2} = 400(u_2 - x_2) + 2000 - 400(255 - u_2) = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad u^*_2 = \frac{x_2 + 250}{2} \]

  • Autumn’s level is between 240 and 255, so \({u^*_2}\) is between 245 and 252.5: above winter’s 200
  • Substituting: \({J^*_2(x_2) = 50(250 - x_2)^2 + 50(260 - x_2)^2 + 1000(x_2 - 150)}\)

The second derivative is 800 > 0, so the stationary point is the minimum. Substitution: u*_2 - x_2 = (250 - x_2)/2 and 255 - u*_2 = (260 - x_2)/2, and 200/4 = 50.

Autumn: The Requirement Binds

\(Q^*_1(x_1, u_1) = 200(u_1 - x_1)^2 + 2000(u_1 - 240) + J^*_2(u_1)\)

\[ \frac{\partial Q^*_1}{\partial u_1} = 400(u_1 - x_1) + 2000 - 100(250 - u_1) - 100(260 - u_1) + 1000 = 0 \]

Solving: \({600u_1 = 400x_1 + 48{,}000}\), so \({u_1 = (2x_1 + 240)/3}\).

  • This is \({\ge 240}\) only if \({x_1 \ge 240}\). Below, \({Q^*_1}\) rises on \({[240, 255]}\), so \({u^*_1 = 240}\)

\[ u^*_1(x_1) = \begin{cases} 240 & 220 \le x_1 \le 240 \\[2pt] (2x_1 + 240)/3 & 240 \le x_1 \le 255 \end{cases} \]

Summer and the Plan

  • Summer: \({\partial Q^*_0/\partial u_0 = 0}\) gives \({u^*_0 = 247.5}\) (appendix). Forward: \({u_1 = 245}\), \({u_2 = 247.5}\), \({u_3 = 255}\)
Total cost $185,000. gurobipy, as a quadratic program: the same plan
Season Level Change Surplus
Summer 247.5 11,250 55,000
Autumn 245 1,250 10,000
Winter 247.5 1,250 95,000
Spring 255 11,250 0

Change cost: 200 x 7.5^2 = 11,250 in summer (255 to 247.5), 200 x 2.5^2 = 1,250 in autumn and winter, 200 x 7.5^2 in spring. Surplus: 2,000 x 27.5, 2,000 x 5, 2,000 x 47.5, 0. The winter surplus is the largest cost and still cheaper than the swings it avoids. The notebook solves this quadratic program.

Probabilistic Recursions: Maximizing a Probability

When Chance Picks the Next State

\[ \begin{alignat*}{2} J^*_k(x_k) & {}= \min_{u_k} E_{w_k}\Big[\, g_k(x_k, u_k, w_k) + J^*_{k+1}\big(f_k(x_k, u_k, w_k)\big) \Big] \\[4pt] & {}= \min_{u_k} \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i \big[\, c_i + J^*_{k+1}(i) \big] \end{alignat*} \]

\({w_k}\): the disturbance; \({p_i}\): probability of state \({i}\); \({c_i}\): the cost on that branch.

Bertsekas’s basic problem: x_k+1 = f_k(x_k, u_k, w_k), with w_k random; its distribution may depend on x_k and u_k, never on earlier w’s. The control fixes the probabilities, and chance picks the next state (Hillier and Lieberman draw it as Fig. 11.10). The recursion takes the expected value over the branches; the principle of optimality still holds, because the best decisions from state i do not depend on how the process got there.

Three Chips, Three Plays

  • A player’s system wins each play with probability \({2/3}\); a bet of \({x}\) chips wins \({x}\) or loses \({x}\)
  • The player starts with 3 chips and wins a side bet with 5 or more after 3 plays. Maximize the probability of winning it
  • Stage \({k}\): play \({k + 1}\); state \({x_k}\): chips in hand; control \({u_k \le x_k}\): chips bet; disturbance \({w_k = +1}\) (win) or \({-1}\): \({x_{k+1} = x_k + w_k u_k}\)

\[ \begin{alignat*}{2} Q^*_k(x_k, u_k) & {}= \tfrac{1}{3}\, J^*_{k+1}(x_k - u_k) + \tfrac{2}{3}\, J^*_{k+1}(x_k + u_k) \\[4pt] J^*_3(x_3) & {}= 1 \text{ if } x_3 \ge 5, \text{ and 0 otherwise} \end{alignat*} \]

Hillier and Lieberman’s Example 6, Winning in Las Vegas. The objective is a probability, so each stage cost is 0 and the terminal value J*_3 is 1 or 0. Ask first: should the player bet everything on play 1?

Plays 3 and 2

x2 0 1 2 3 4

k = 0 ⅓ J1*(x0 − u0) + ⅔ J1*(x0 + u0) J0*(x0) u0*
x0 0 1 2 3

Play Chips Bet

Probability 20/27 ≈ 0.74

Bet 1 chip, then adapt: the bet at play 2 depends on what play 1 did. Betting everything at once wins only 2/3.

“Enough to reach 5”: with 3 chips bet 2 or 3; with 4 chips bet 1 to 4. With 2 chips or fewer at play 3 the side bet is lost. Check by the tree: 2/3 [2/3 + 1/3 x 2/3] + 1/3 x 4/9 = 16/27 + 4/27 = 20/27.

Expected-Cost Recursions: A State-Dependent Policy

Two Engines, Three Auctions

  • A repair shop needs two refurbished engines within three weeks
  • One engine is auctioned each week: skip, bid low or bid high. The shop pays only if it wins
  • After week 3, each missing engine costs 14 new from the dealer
  • Minimize the expected total cost
Bid Price ($1,000s) Wins
Low 3 \({1/2}\)
High 6 \({3/4}\)

Written for this course. Bidding high costs more but wins more often; skipping saves the bid and spends a week. The dealer’s price is the penalty for running out of time.

The Recursion

  • Stage \({k}\): week \({k + 1}\); state \({x_k}\): engines still needed (0, 1, 2); control \({u_k}\): skip, low or high
  • A bid \({b}\) that wins with probability \({p}\):

\[ \begin{alignat*}{2} Q^*_k(x_k, b) & {}= p\,\big[\, b + J^*_{k+1}(x_k - 1) \,\big] + (1 - p)\, J^*_{k+1}(x_k) \\[4pt] Q^*_k(x_k, \text{skip}) & {}= J^*_{k+1}(x_k) && \qquad J^*_3(x_3) = 14x_3 \end{alignat*} \]

  • Each branch has its own stage cost: the bid if won, 0 if lost
  • \({J^*_k}\) is an expected cost: the algorithm takes a minimum of averages

Weeks 3 and 2

2 28 ½(3 + 14) + ½(28) = 22.5 ¾(6 + 14) + ¼(28) = 22 22 High

x1 Skip Low High
0 0 0 none

2 22 ½(3 + 8) + ½(22) = 16.5 ¾(6 + 8) + ¼(22) = 16 16 High

Week 3, one engine needed: low costs 1/2(3 + 0) + 1/2(14) = 8.5, high 3/4(6 + 0) + 1/4(14) = 8. With the dealer at 14, the higher chance is worth the higher price. Week 2, one engine: low wins 5.5 against 6.5, because a loss still leaves week 3.

Bid low while time remains; bid high when the deadline is near and engines are missing. Buying both from the dealer costs $28,000.

The policy is a rule by week and state: the decision in week 2 depends on what happened in week 1. No fixed plan of three bids, chosen in advance, can match it. Week 1, two needed: low 12.25, high 12.625, skip 16.

Part III: Markov Decision Processes and Reinforcement Learning

When there is no last stage, and when the probabilities must be learned

Markov Decision Processes and the Bellman Equation

A Shop with No Last Week

  • A shop sells a premium espresso machine. Each Monday it sees its stock \({i}\) (the room holds 3) and orders \({u}\) units; they arrive at once
  • Weekly demand is 0, 1 or 2 with probabilities \({1/4}\), \({1/2}\), \({1/4}\); a sale missed is lost
Sale price Unit cost Per order Per unit left on Sunday
$800 $400 $200 $100
  • No week is the last: a dollar next week is worth \({\alpha = 0.8}\) today. Equivalently, each week the product stays on sale with probability 0.8
  • Decide how much to order in each state, for every week

Written for this course. In $100s: price 8, cost 4, fee 2, holding 1. The discount factor can be read as interest or as the chance the product line survives another week; both give the same model.

Markov Decision Process

Markov decision process (MDP)

States \({i}\); controls \({u \in U(i)}\); transition probabilities \({p_{ij}(u)}\); expected stage profit \({g(i, u)}\); discount factor \({0 \le \alpha < 1}\). The next state depends only on the current state and control.

  • A stationary policy \({\mu}\) names a control for each state, the same every week
  • Its value: \({J_\mu(i) = E\big[\sum_{k \ge 0} \alpha^k\, g(x_k, \mu(x_k)) \mid x_0 = i\big]}\)
The shop as an MDP
State \({i}\) Control \({u}\) Profit \({g(i, u)}\)
Stock on Monday, 0 to 3 Units ordered, \({u \le 3 - i}\) Sales minus holding and order cost

The Shop’s Data

Everything after the order depends only on the stock \({y = i + u}\):

Stock y Expected sales Expected left R(y) = 8 sales − left Next stock 0 Next stock 1 Next stock 2 Next stock 3
0 0 0 0 1
1 0.75 0.25 5.75 ¾ ¼
2 1 1 7 ¼ ½ ¼
3 1 2 6 ¼ ½ ¼
  • Next stock: probabilities from the demand. Profit: \({g(i, u) = R(i + u) - (2 + 4u)}\) if \({u > 0}\), and \({R(i)}\) if \({u = 0}\)

Example, y = 2: sales are 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 1/4, 1/2, 1/4, mean 1; units left 2, 1, 0, mean 1. So R(2) = 8 - 1 = 7. A third unit never sells in the week it arrives (demand is at most 2), so R(3) = 6 < 7; it is worth stocking only for next week.

The Bellman Equation

\[ J^*(i) = \max_{u \in U(i)} \Big[\, g(i, u) + \alpha \sum_{j} p_{ij}(u)\, J^*(j) \Big] \qquad \text{for every } i \]

  • Part II’s DP algorithm with the stage index dropped: every week looks the same, so \({J^*_k}\) becomes one function \({J^*}\)
  • Four equations in four unknowns, with a max: no direct solve

Two ways to solve it

Value iteration: apply the right-hand side again and again. Linear programming: the smallest \({J}\) that satisfies every “\({\ge}\)” version of the equation.

Bellman (1957) wrote the stationary equation as well as the finite-stage recursion. alpha < 1 keeps the sum of discounted profits finite. Bertsekas writes Bellman’s equation for costs, with min; the shop maximizes profit, so max takes its place.

Value Iteration and Linear Programming

Value Iteration

  1. Start from \({J_0(i) = 0}\) for every \({i}\)
  2. Sweep: \({J_{k+1}(i) = \max_u \big[ g(i, u) + \alpha \sum_j p_{ij}(u)\, J_k(j) \big]}\)
  3. Stop when \({\max_i |J_{k+1}(i) - J_k(i)|}\) is small; act greedily on \({J_{k+1}}\)
  • \({J_k}\) is the best expected profit over \({k}\) weeks: \({k}\) stages of Part II
  • Each sweep cuts the error at least by the factor \({\alpha}\): after \({k}\) sweeps it is at most \({\alpha^k}\) times the first error

One sweep for the shop, in two steps

\({G_k(y) = R(y) + 0.8 \sum_j P(j \mid y)\, J_k(j)}\), then \({J_{k+1}(i) = \max_{y \ge i} \{ G_k(y) - \text{order cost} \}}\), with order cost \({2 + 4(y - i)}\) if \({y > i}\)

Sweep 1 by Hand

\({J_0 = 0}\), so \({G_0(y) = R(y)}\): 0, 5.75, 7, 6.

sweep 1 G0(y) − order cost, by stock after ordering y J1(i) order
i 0 1 2 3
0 0 5.75 − 6 = −0.25 7 − 10 = −3 6 − 14 = −8 0 0
1 5.75 7 − 6 = 1 6 − 10 = −4 5.75 0
2 7 6 − 6 = 0 7 0
3 6 6 0

With one week left, ordering never pays

A unit bought for $400 plus the $200 fee cannot earn it back in one week: \({5.75 - 6 < 0}\) from an empty shelf.

Row i = 0: no order gives 0; ordering 1 gives R(1) - (2 + 4) = -0.25; ordering 2 gives 7 - 10 = -3; ordering 3 gives 6 - 14 = -8. J_1 is the best expected profit if the world ended after this week.

Sweep 2 by Hand

y R(y) 0.8 × expected J(next) G(y)
0 0 0.8(0) = 0 0
1 5.75 0.2(5.75) + 0.6(0) = 1.15 6.9
2 7 0.2(7) + 0.4(5.75) + 0.2(0) = 3.7 10.7
3 6 0.2(6) + 0.4(7) + 0.2(5.75) = 5.15 11.15
sweep 2 G1(y) − order cost, by stock after ordering y J2(i) order
i 0 1 2 3
0 0 6.9 − 6 = 0.9 10.7 − 10 = 0.7 11.15 − 14 = −2.85 0.9 1
1 6.9 10.7 − 6 = 4.7 11.15 − 10 = 1.15 6.9 0
2 10.7 11.15 − 6 = 5.15 10.7 0
3 11.15 11.15 0

Weights: 0.8 x 1/4 = 0.2 and 0.8 x 1/2 = 0.4. y = 2: 7 + 0.2 J_1(2) + 0.4 J_1(1) + 0.2 J_1(0) = 7 + 1.4 + 2.3 + 0 = 10.7. With two weeks counted, an empty shop orders 1: 6.9 - 6 = 0.9 > 0. From sweep 3 on it orders 2.

The Optimal Policy

Exact values by solving the Bellman equation for this policy
Stock \({i}\) \({J^*(i)}\) ($100s) Order
0 6.25 2

Order 2 when the shelf is empty

A reorder point of 0 and an order-up-to level of 2: an \({(s, S)}\) policy. The fee makes small, frequent orders expensive.

  • The policy settled at sweep 3; the values took 31 sweeps to come within 0.01 of \({J^*}\)

J(2) - J(0) = 10 exactly: from 0, ordering 2 costs 2 + 8 = 10 and leaves the shop in the same position as starting with 2. Exact values: 25/4, 95/8, 65/4, 595/32.

The Bellman Equation as an LP

\[ \begin{alignat*}{3} \min~ & \rlap{\textstyle\sum_i J(i)} \\[4pt] \text{s.t.}~ & J(i) - \alpha \textstyle\sum_{j} p_{ij}(u)\, J(j) & \quad & {}\ge g(i, u) && \qquad \text{every } i, u \end{alignat*} \]

  • \({J(i)}\) free in sign. One variable per state, one constraint per state and control: 4 and 10 for the shop
  • gurobipy: \({J = (6.25, 11.875, 16.25, 18.59)}\); the tight constraints are the optimal controls

Lecture 04 again

The dual’s variables are discounted state-action frequencies: how often the policy applies control \({u}\) in state \({i}\). Weak and strong duality hold as for any LP.

Any J that satisfies all “>=” constraints is an upper bound on J, so the smallest one is J. The four tight rows are (i=0, order 2) and (i, order 0) for i = 1, 2, 3. The notebook builds this LP.

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def J(k, x):
    if k == len(loads):
        return 0
    name, a, v = loads[k]
    return max(J(k + 1, x), v + J(k + 1, x - a)) if a <= x else J(k + 1, x)

Reinforcement Learning: Q-Learning from Samples

When the Probabilities Are Unknown

  • Value iteration needs \({p_{ij}(u)}\). A new product has no demand history
  • The Q-factor of a state and control: \({Q^*(i, u) = g(i, u) + \alpha \sum_j p_{ij}(u)\, J^*(j)}\)
  • Then \({J^*(i) = \max_u Q^*(i, u)}\), and the best control is the \({u}\) that attains it

Learn Q from experience

Each week shows one sample: state \({i}\), control \({u}\), profit \({g}\), next state \({j}\). Reinforcement learning estimates \({Q^*}\) from such samples, without writing \({p_{ij}(u)}\) down.

Q-Learning

After each observed step \({(i, u, g, j)}\):

\[ Q(i, u) \leftarrow Q(i, u) + \gamma \Big[\, g + \alpha \max_{v \in U(j)} Q(j, v) - Q(i, u) \,\Big] \]

  • The bracket is the error in the Bellman equation, measured on one sample
  • \({\gamma}\): the step size, or learning rate; \({\alpha}\) is still the discount
  • Explore: now and then try an action other than the best so far

Watkins and Dayan (1992)

Q-learning converges to \({Q^*}\) if every state-control pair is tried infinitely often and the step sizes shrink suitably.

Same equation as value iteration; the expectation over j is replaced by the one j the world produced, and the step size gamma averages the samples over time. Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis (Neuro-Dynamic Programming) also write the step size as gamma. No code here: the idea is what matters for the exam.

Powell’s Unified Framework

Every sequential decision problem has five parts (Powell, 2019, 2022):

Part Powell Bertsekas The shop
State \({S_t}\) \({x_k}\) Stock on Monday
Decision \({x_t}\) \({u_k}\) Units ordered
New information \({W_{t+1}}\) \({w_k}\) The week’s demand
Transition \({S^M(S_t, x_t, W_{t+1})}\) \({f_k(x_k, u_k, w_k)}\) Stock left on Sunday
Objective Over policies \({X^\pi}\) Over policies \({\mu}\) Expected discounted profit
  • Four classes of policies: rules, modified deterministic models, value function approximations (this lecture), lookaheads (lecture 05)

A rule for the shop: order up to 2. Lookaheads include lecture 05’s stochastic programs. Powell’s x_t is the decision and Bertsekas’s x_k the state: the letters swap between the two books.

Sutton and Barto: Reinforcement Learning

  • An agent acts in an environment, receives rewards and learns a policy by trial and error; the MDP is the model behind it
  • Three families: value-based (Q-learning), policy-based (adjust the policy along the gradient of its value), model-based (learn \({p}\), then plan)
  • When the states are too many to list, a function approximates \({J}\) or \({Q}\); with a neural network, this is deep reinforcement learning

The bridge

The Bellman equation of this lecture is the equation those methods solve, from samples, when the transition probabilities are unknown.

Sutton and Barto (2018) is the standard text. Powell’s framework and Sutton and Barto’s book describe the same problem class from operations research and from computer science.

Where Sequential Decisions Appear

Schneider National’s fleet planning used approximate dynamic programming (Simão et al., 2009); backgammon (Tesauro, 1995) and Go (Silver et al., 2016) by reinforcement learning
Application State Decision
Inventory Stock on hand Units to order
Revenue management Seats left, days to departure Fares to offer
Maintenance Condition of a machine Repair, replace or wait
Truckload fleets Drivers and loads by city Which driver takes which load
Games Board position Next move

Conclusions

Summary of Part I

Core takeaways

  • Stages, states, controls; the DP algorithm \({J^*_k(x_k) = \min_{u_k} [g_k + J^*_{k+1}(f_k)]}\)
  • Solve backward, read forward
  • The answer is a policy \({\mu_k(x_k)}\); any \({g_k}\) works

Watch out for

  • Ties: keep every \({u^*_k}\), they branch the forward pass
  • Infeasible decisions: leave the cell blank
  • A vector state: the states multiply

Summary of Part II

Core takeaways

  • Continuous state: \({J^*_k}\) is a formula; endpoints or calculus
  • Probabilistic: \({J^*_k = \min_{u_k} E_{w_k}[g_k + J^*_{k+1}]}\)
  • The answer is a policy: a decision for each state

Watch out for

  • Start-up costs break linearity at 0
  • Check that a stationary point is feasible
  • Each branch has its own stage cost

Summary of Part III

Core takeaways

  • No last stage: discount, drop \({k}\), Bellman’s equation
  • Value iteration converges; the policy often settles first
  • The MDP is also an LP

Watch out for

  • \({\alpha < 1}\) is what keeps values finite
  • Q-learning trades the model for samples and exploration

Bottom line

Name the stages and the state first; the recursion follows from them.

Appendix: Summer by Calculus

For \({x_1 \ge 240}\), the slope of \({J^*_1}\) is that of its first term at \({u^*_1}\):

\[ \frac{d J^*_1}{d x_1} = -400\,(u^*_1 - x_1) = -400 \Big( \frac{2x_1 + 240}{3} - x_1 \Big) = \frac{400}{3}(x_1 - 240) \]

With \({x_1 = u_0}\):

\[ \frac{\partial Q^*_0}{\partial u_0} = 400(u_0 - 255) + 2000 + \frac{400}{3}(u_0 - 240) = 0 \]

Times 3: \({1200u_0 - 306{,}000 + 6{,}000 + 400u_0 - 96{,}000 = 0}\), so \({1600u_0 = 396{,}000}\) and \({u^*_0 = 247.5}\).

  • On \({220 \le u_0 \le 240}\) the slope is \({800u_0 - 196{,}000 < 0}\): no minimum there
